rows.title: The incremental conjecture for set multipartite Ramsey numbers
rows.record_statement:
Let $s\geq 2$ and $n\geq 2$ be integers. For positive integers $s,n$, let $M_s(n)$ denote the set multipartite Ramsey number for $C_4$ versus the star $K_{1,n}$, namely the least $c$ such that every spanning subgraph $G$ of the complete balanced $s$-partite graph $K_{c\times s}$ contains a copy of $C_4$ or its complement contains a copy of $K_{1,n}$. **Incremental conjecture.** For any integers $s\geq 2$ and $n\geq 2$, 
$$
M_s(n+1)\leq M_s(n)+1.
$$
 The preceding proposition proves this bound under an additional numerical hypothesis; the conjecture asserts that the hypothesis can be removed.
rows.source: Claudia J. F. Gonçalves, Emerson L. Monte Carmelo and Irene N. Nakaoka, “Projective planes and set multipartite Ramsey numbers for C_4 versus star”, arXiv:1710.06383 (2017).
rows.what_was_proved: For all s >= 2 and n >= 2, M_s(n+1) <= M_s(n) + 1, where M_s(n) is the least positive c such that every spanning subgraph G of the complete multipartite graph with c classes of s vertices either contains a 4-cycle or leaves some vertex with at least n non-neighbours in other classes (a star K_{1,n} in the complement relative to the host). This is Conjecture 2.3 of Goncalves, Monte Carmelo and Nakaoka, who proved the inequality only under an additional numerical hypothesis by keeping the original partition. The proof here proves the stronger step that the property at (n, c) implies the property at (n+1, c+1) by abandoning the partition: delete s suitable vertices and re-partition the rest into c independent s-sets, by a one-vertex swap forced by C4-freeness when s >= 3, and for s = 2 by a friendship-type lemma (two vertices with no common neighbour) with a perfect matching in the complement, plus explicit small cases. Lean defines the host graph, the property and the minimum literally, and proves that the minimum exists.

rows.title: The half-length uniqueness conjecture for bi-roots
rows.record_statement:
Let $w$ be a primitive word. A **bi-root** of $w$ is a primitive pair $\{x,y\}$ whose concatenations include $w$. **The half-length uniqueness conjecture.** The word $w$ has at most one bi-root $\{x,y\}$ such that

$$
|x|+|y|<\frac{|w|}{2}.
$$

The preceding theorem proves the analogous uniqueness statement under the stronger bound $|x|+|y|<\sqrt{|w|}$. The supplied text presents the half-length bound as a problem related to the first conjecture, but gives no resolution.
rows.source: Giuseppa Castiglione, Gabriele Fici and Antonio Restivo, “Primitive Sets of Words”, arXiv:2005.10668 (2020).
rows.what_was_proved: A primitive word w over a finite alphabet has at most one bi-root of at most half its length: if X and U are primitive pairs (two-element bases of 2-maximal submonoids) that both generate w, and twice the total length of each is below |w|, then X = U. This is the half-length uniqueness conjecture of Castiglione, Fici and Restivo, who proved uniqueness only under a square-root length bound. The proof establishes their additive conjecture in a stronger form: two distinct primitive pairs generating the same primitive word have total length at least |w| + 3. It folds the two generator graphs, glues them along the path of w into a graph of rank at most 3, shows that in rank 3 a cycle of the incidence graph would give w a period, so that the incidence graph is a forest and the bound follows by counting, and treats the remaining case by recoding w through first returns and a weighted induction on length that changes the alphabet. Lean states primitive words, generated submonoids, 2-maximality and primitive pairs literally.

rows.title: The $3$-cube-free density conjecture in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$
rows.record_statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer, and consider subsets of $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ that contain no $3$-cube. **The $3$-cube-free density conjecture.** The largest $3$-cube-free family in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$ has size $(5/8)\cdot 2^n$. Since $L_1\cup L_3$ is $3$-cube-free, the proposed bound would be sharp; the paper states that this is the first open case of the general optimality conjecture.
rows.source: Jason Long and Adam Zsolt Wagner, “The largest projective cube-free subsets of Z_2^n”, arXiv:1810.01225 (2018).
rows.what_was_proved: A subset A of the cyclic group Z_{2^n} that contains no 3-dimensional cube, that is no x, y, z (not necessarily distinct, zero allowed) with all seven nonempty subset sums in A, has at most (5/8) 2^n elements, and for every n >= 3 the maximum is exactly 5 * 2^(n-3). This is Conjecture 5.1 of Long and Wagner. The earlier upper bounds were 2/3 (Meng) and, three days before this result, a treatment of the case where the odd layer has density above 2/3 (Randjelovic), with the interval between 5/8 and 2/3 left open. The proof averages a certified weighted inequality for cube-free sets over odd multipliers, decomposes the density by 2-adic layers, treats the high-odd-density branch by a direct counting argument, and inducts over the subgroups 16Z and 32Z; the extremal example is the preimage of five residues modulo 8. The finite inequality is certified by one verified checker over 12,564 states and 1,441 cubes, with the coverage of all cases proved in Lean.

rows.title: Strong-product immersion conjecture
rows.record_statement:
Let $G$ and $H$ be graphs, and write $\operatorname{im}(G)=t$ and $\operatorname{im}(H)=r$. **Strong-product immersion conjecture.** Then

$$
\operatorname{im}(G\boxtimes H)\geq tr.
$$
 This conjecture is motivated by the identity $K_t\boxtimes K_r=K_{tr}$ and the resulting immersion number of the strong product of complete graphs; the paper presents it as an unresolved conjecture.
rows.source: Karen L. Collins, Megan E. Heenehan and Jessica McDonald, “Clique immersion in graph products”, arXiv:1908.10457 (2019).
rows.what_was_proved: The conjecture that the immersion number is supermultiplicative for the strong product, im(G) im(H) <= im(G ⊠ H), is false. Let F_a be the complete bipartite graph K_{a,a} with, on each side, one extra vertex shared by each perfect matching (a compressed form of adding a matching). With G = F_4 on 14 vertices and H = F_6 on 22 vertices, im(G) = 8 and im(H) = 12, but K_96 does not immerse in the 308-vertex product G ⊠ H: only 96 vertices of the product have degree at least 95, so they would have to be the branch vertices, and a checkerboard cut separating them 48 against 48 has 2,224 edges while 48 * 48 = 2,304 edge-disjoint paths would have to cross it. Lean defines weak immersions, the immersion number and the strong product, proves the two immersion numbers, the degree and cut counts, and derives the negation of the universal statement.

rows.title: Switch-generation conjecture for the matching preorder
rows.record_statement:
Let $\mathcal{M}_n$ be the set of the labelled perfect matchings under consideration, and let $\preceq$ be the preorder on this set. A **switch** is the local transformation defined earlier in the paper. **Switch-generation conjecture.** If $N,M\in\mathcal{M}_n$ satisfy $N\preceq M$, then there exists a sequence

$$
N=M_1\preceq M_2\preceq\dots\preceq M_{k-1}\preceq M_k=M
$$

such that $M_j$ is a switch of $M_{j+1}$ for every $j$. This is presented as an open conjecture about whether the preorder is generated by switches; the supplied parser gives no evidence of resolution.
rows.source: Joseph Briggs, Jessica McDonald and Songling Shan, “Degree sequences realizing labelled perfect matchings”, arXiv:2510.01110 (2025).
rows.what_was_proved: For perfect matchings N and M of the vertex set {1, ..., n}, write N ⪯ M when every weakly decreasing degree sequence that has a realization containing M also has one containing N. If N ⪯ M then there is a chain N = M_1 ⪯ M_2 ⪯ ... ⪯ M_k = M in which each step is one of the three switches of the source. This is Conjecture 11 of Briggs, McDonald and Shan. The proof shows that the preorder is the reverse Bruhat order on fixed-point-free involutions: a new separating-graph lemma produces, whenever a crossing-count inequality fails, a degree sequence realized with M but not with N; a direct induction on rank defects then moves from N toward M one switch at a time, and the source's Lemma 10(b) keeps every step inside the preorder. Lean defines matchings as edge sets, realizability by actual simple graphs with prescribed degrees, and the three switch types literally.

rows.title: Gago–Coroničová-Hurajová–Madaras conjecture on low-betweenness uniform graphs
rows.record_statement: Let $G$ be a **low-betweenness BUG**, meaning a betweenness-uniform graph whose betweenness value is less than $1$. Write $\overline{G}$ for its complement. **Gago–Coroničová-Hurajová–Madaras conjecture.** If $G$ is a low-betweenness BUG, then its complement $\overline{G}$ is a disjoint union of stars of the same size. This would classify the low-betweenness betweenness-uniform graphs and show that the construction from disjoint unions of equally sized stars yields all such examples. The conjecture is presented as open in the source.
rows.source: Babak Ghanbari, David Hartman, Vít Jelínek, Aneta Pokorná, Robert Šámal and Pavel Valtr, “Structure of betweenness uniform graphs with low values of betweenness centrality”, arXiv:2401.00347 (2023).
rows.what_was_proved: A connected graph in which every vertex has the same betweenness centrality, with that common value below 1, is the complement of a disjoint union of stars K_{1,l} of one common size l. This is Conjecture 2 of Ghanbari, Hartman, Jelinek, Pokorna, Samal and Valtr (the MathDB record's title credits other authors, whose different conjecture that paper disproved). The source proved the statement for components that are themselves uniform (its Theorem 17) and excluded small l case by case. The proof here replaces uniformity by Jensen's inequality in the source's excess argument and adds one new lemma, that every vertex is close to at least l + 1 edges of the complement, together with the equality case. Lean defines betweenness by counting shortest walks over unordered pairs of other vertices, proves the shortest-walk counting the argument needs, and includes guard theorems against the wrong normalizations.

rows.title: Parity congruence conjecture for finite Mordell--Tornheim sums
rows.record_statement:
Let $r\in\N$, let $p$ be a prime, and let $\bfs\in\N^d$ satisfy $p>|\bfs|+1$, where $|\bfs|$ is the weight and $Z_{p^r}(\bfs)$ is the corresponding finite Mordell--Tornheim sum. **Finite Mordell--Tornheim congruence conjecture.** The following congruences should hold:

1. If $d=4$ and $|\bfs|$ is odd, then

$$
Z_{p^r}(\bfs)\equiv p^{2r-2}Z_p(\bfs)\pmod{p^{2r-1}}.
$$

2. If $d=4$ and $|\bfs|$ is even, then

$$
Z_{p^r}(\bfs)\equiv p^{r-1}Z_p(\bfs)\pmod{p^r}.
$$

3. If $d=5$ and $|\bfs|$ is even, then

$$
Z_{p^r}(\bfs)\equiv p^{2r-2}Z_p(\bfs)\pmod{p^{2r-1}}.
$$

In general, if $r\geq2$ and $d+|\bfs|$ is odd, then

$$
Z_{p^r}(\bfs)\equiv0\pmod{p^{2r-2}};
$$

if $r\geq2$ and $d+|\bfs|$ is even, then

$$
Z_{p^r}(\bfs)\equiv0\pmod{p^{r-1}}.
$$

The conjecture extends parity-dependent congruences for finite Mordell--Tornheim sums beyond the cases proved earlier in the paper. It is supported by extensive numerical evidence, while the stated general assertions remain open.
rows.source: Crystal Wang and Jianqiang Zhao, “Mordell–Tornheim Zeta Values, Their Alternating Version, and Their Finite Analogs”, arXiv:2401.03380 (2024).
rows.what_was_proved: All five assertions of Conjecture 3.4 of Wang and Zhao hold: for a prime p exceeding the weight plus one, every r >= 1 and every exponent vector s of positive integers, the finite sums Z_{p^r}^{d}(s) over compositions of p^r into d positive parts prime to p satisfy the stated divisibility by powers of p, the scaling laws in depths 4 and 5 relating level p^{r+1} to level p^r, and the general recurrence in r. Earlier work (Chen and Zhao; McCoy, Thielen, Wang and Zhao) treated only exponents all equal to 1, where just the last assertion applies; the source proved depth 3 by Bernoulli-number computations. The proof lifts the sum from level p^r to p^{r+1} keeping double precision (modulus p^{2r+1}), shows that the second moments of the carries vanish modulo p, and projects onto one reflection parity to gain a further factor of p. Lean states the sums and the five congruences literally in the integers modulo prime powers.

rows.title: The minimal surjective-strategy conjecture for wreath products
rows.record_statement: Let $G\wr H$ be a wreath product with state group $K$, and call a surjective strategy **minimal** when it has the form $\{k_i\in K\}_{i=1}^{|K|-1}$. **Minimal strategy conjecture.** Whenever $G\wr H$ has a surjective strategy, it also has a minimal surjective strategy $\{k_i\in K\}_{i=1}^{|K|-1}$. Minimal strategies would give the shortest possible guaranteed bound discussed in the source; the conjecture is based on the examples known to the authors and remains open.
rows.source: Peter Kagey, “Spinning switches on a wreath product”, arXiv:2210.09408 (2022).
rows.what_was_proved: For a generalized spinning-switches puzzle with switch group G, a finite set of positions on which the adversary's group H acts, and state group K = G^Ω: if a strategy (a fixed sequence of moves that reaches every state whatever the adversary does) exists, then one of the minimal possible length |K| - 1 exists. This is Conjecture 41 of Kagey. The proof classifies when a strategy exists at all: only when |K| = 1, when H acts trivially, or when G and the image of H are p-groups for the same prime p. The new part is the obstruction: an invariant on cosets of p-subgroups shows that a switch group that is not a p-group can never win, in cases the source's quotient argument does not reach (for example A_5). For p-groups a minimal strategy is built by induction through a central subgroup of order p fixed by H. Lean defines the puzzle through the actual semidirect product, includes the initial state, and proves by computation that a strategy exists in a small nontrivial case and does not exist for S_3.

rows.title: The forbidden-pattern characterization conjecture for one-stack one-queue layouts
rows.record_statement:
Let an ordered matching have a fixed non-separated layout. A **$1$-stack $1$-queue layout** uses one stack and one queue, and a **mixed layout on $1$ page** uses one page whose edges may be assigned to stacks or queues. The twelve and eight patterns referred to below are the patterns depicted in the source's figures.

**Forbidden-pattern characterization conjecture.** The ordered matching admits

$$
\text{a $1$-stack $1$-queue layout if and only if it avoids the 12 patterns depicted in the source's figure,}
$$

and admits a mixed layout on one page if and only if it avoids the 8 patterns depicted in the source's figure.

This conjecture proposes complete finite obstruction sets for the two smallest non-separated layout classes. It is consistent with the preceding computational enumeration of twelve and eight critical matchings, but the supplied source gives no proof or resolution.
rows.source: Deborah Haun, Laura Merker and Sergey Pupyrev, “Forbidden Patterns in Mixed Linear Layouts”, arXiv:2412.12786 (2024).
rows.what_was_proved: Both characterizations of Conjecture 31 hold for every finite ordered matching. The content is part (i): with the vertex order fixed, deciding a 1-stack 1-queue layout is a 2-SAT problem, whose contradiction cycles can be arbitrarily long, so 2-SAT alone gives no finite obstruction set. The proof shows that for intervals, three-edge forcing configurations plus propagation decide colourability, and that the geometry of intervals shortens every contradiction path to at most one link. Hence every matching without such a layout contains one with at most six edges, and an enumeration of the 11,465 matchings with at most six edges gives exactly the 12 patterns of Figure 19a. Part (ii) is routine (a failure needs a crossing pair and a nesting pair, at most four edges; also the source's Lemma 27). Lean defines ordered matchings on natural-number endpoints, layouts as the source does, and containment as an injective edge map preserving every endpoint comparison; the figure patterns are literal endpoint tables; no size cap enters the statement.

rows.title: The three conjectural sporadics in the entropic order on a parabolic quotient of $S_6$
rows.record_statement:
In the above notation, let the displayed arrays denote the corresponding elements of the parabolic quotient, and let $\rhd$ denote the entropic partial order.

**Three sporadic entropic-order conjectures.** The following three relations hold:

$$
\begin{array}{rcl}
\mathbf{37}\rhd\mathbf{11}:\quad \left(\begin{array}{ccc}a & c & f\\b & d & e\end{array}\right)&\rhd&\left(\begin{array}{ccc}a & b & d\\f & c & e\end{array}\right),\\
\mathbf{43}\rhd\mathbf{11}:\quad \left(\begin{array}{ccc}a & d & e\\b & c & f\end{array}\right)&\rhd&\left(\begin{array}{ccc}a & b & d\\f & c & e\end{array}\right),\\
\mathbf{49}\rhd\mathbf{11}:\quad \left(\begin{array}{ccc}a & d & f\\b & c & e\end{array}\right)&\rhd&\left(\begin{array}{ccc}a & b & d\\f & c & e\end{array}\right).
\end{array}
$$

These are the remaining sporadic relations identified in the paper; the preceding discussion explains that the author was unable to prove them and that their structure does not yield to the techniques used for the other relations.
rows.source: Gary McConnell, “An entropic partial order on a parabolic quotient of S6”, arXiv:1209.2674 (2012).
rows.what_was_proved: All three relations hold on the whole closed ordered domain, ties and zero entries included. Arguments that use only convexity of x log x (majorization, Schur concavity, Karamata) cannot work, because the inequalities fail when x log x is replaced by x squared, as the source remarks, and the author wrote that these three relations do not yield to the identric-mean technique that proved the others. The proof reduces to a = b by the sign of the derivative in a, uses concavity along a direction that keeps the positive marginals fixed to reduce to five faces of the domain, treats each face by one-variable monotonicity, and on the hardest face uses a weighted gradient bound (log x >= 1 - 1/x with an explicit nonnegative polynomial) followed along the curves A/C^2 = constant. Lean states the mutual information with Mathlib's negMulLog, keeps the joint-entropy term, fixes the direction of the order, and writes the four arrays out explicitly.
